system.description: Humans are restless, adaptable, and ambitious, making much of their brief lives and finding strength in one another.

lore.label: Summary
lore.text: Humans are restless, adaptable, and ambitious, making much of their brief lives and finding strength in one another.

lore.label: About
lore.text:
Humans are everywhere, and everywhere they are different. No other people spreads so far, argues so loudly, or reinvents itself so often. A human border town can change its laws, its faith, and its skyline inside a single generation; an elf who naps through a decade returns to find the maps redrawn. What humans lack in long memory they repay in momentum, and the other peoples watch them with a mix of admiration and alarm.

That restlessness is personal as much as cultural. A human feels the shortness of their years and answers it with ambition: one more field cleared, one more deal struck, one more mountain nobody sensible would climb. At their best, humans bind strangers into companies and companies into causes. At their worst, they burn through places, promises, and people the way they burn through years.

lore.label: If you want...
lore.text: If you want a character who can come from anywhere, get along with anyone, and refuse to stay in any lane, you should play a human.

lore.label: You Might...
lore.text:
• Chase a goal so hard that rest starts to feel like theft.
• Collect skills, contacts, and causes the way others collect coins.
• Assume any problem can be solved if you just find the right people for it.

lore.label: Others Probably...
lore.text:
• Envy how quickly you learn, adapt, and move on.
• Wonder what you are running from, or racing toward.
• Trust your knack for finding common ground, even between old enemies.

lore.label: Physical Description (at a glance)
lore.text: Humans are middling in most measures and wildly varied in all of them. They stand roughly five to six and a half feet tall, in every build from wiry to broad, with skin, hair, and eyes spanning every shade their homelands offer. What marks a human crowd is not a shared look but a shared motion: quick eyes, busy hands, and clothing that borrows freely from every neighbor they have ever traded with.

lore.label: Physical Description (lifecycle)
lore.text: Humans reach physical adulthood around 15 years and are usually granted a place at the adults' table by 18, though every town draws that line differently. A human who avoids war, plague, and their own ambition can expect sixty to ninety years, and a rare few see a century. Their short season is the quiet engine of their character; humans plant orchards whose shade they will never sit in, and they know it.

lore.label: Society
lore.text:
Human society is less a single design than a permanent argument about what the design should be. Kingdoms, leagues, free towns, wandering companies: humans have tried them all, usually at the same time, usually within a week's ride of each other. Their gift is the joining of strangers. A human market will seat a dwarven smith beside an elven dyer and a gnomish clockmaker, and by closing time the three will share a ledger and a grudge against the harbormaster.

Because they invent themselves so freely, humans put enormous weight on names, oaths, and reputations, the few things that outlive them. A human's word, once given before witnesses, is a load-bearing wall; whole towns stand on webs of such promises. Breaking one is not just a sin but a kind of vandalism.

Humans honor their dead by continuing their projects. Workshops, farms, feuds, and half-built bridges pass from hand to hand like torches, and a human family can often recite what each generation added to the house even when they have forgotten the builders' faces.

lore.label: Beliefs
lore.text: Human belief runs hot and plural. One village keeps six shrines and hedges its bets at all of them; the next follows a single creed with terrifying focus. What is consistent is the human conviction that effort matters, that the world is unfinished, and that somebody, probably them, ought to get on with finishing it. Their prayers tend to be practical: strength for the harvest, luck for the crossing, courage for the morning.

lore.label: Popular Edicts
lore.text:
• Leave every place better than you found it.
• Keep your word once witnesses have heard it.
• Lift the newcomer; you were one once.

lore.label: Popular Anathemas
lore.text:
• Waste a year owed to the people who raised you.
• Break a promise made before witnesses.
• Let fear of failing keep you from beginning.

lore.label: Names
lore.text:
Human given names vary widely between families and homelands. Many human surnames preserve an ancestor’s occupation, carrying the memory of a workshop, livelihood, or useful skill through generations. A family named Cooper might have stopped making barrels centuries ago, yet still treasure the name.
• Common given names Alden, Bram, Cassia, Doran, Elsbeth, Garron, Hale, Imre, Joss, Lysa, Mara, Oren, Sera, Tavin, Wren, Ysolde.
• Common surnames Baker, Carter, Cooper, Fletcher, Mason, Miller, Roper, Tanner, Turner, Weaver.

Dwarves are enduring and powerfully built, with long memories for the things that hold a life together and the faults that can bring it down.

lore.label: Summary
lore.text: Dwarves are enduring and powerfully built, with long memories for the things that hold a life together and the faults that can bring it down.

lore.label: About
lore.text:
A dwarf is difficult to hurry when they think the next step deserves another look. They can feel the strain in a carried load, set their weight before a hard pull, and continue a task long after its novelty has worn away. Outsiders often call this stubbornness. Sometimes the dwarf agrees.

Long life and a durable body make endurance familiar, but they do not make every dwarf patient or every attachment wise. Some stay with a failing work because leaving would feel like admitting it was never worth the effort. Others become adventurers when they finally distinguish what is theirs to carry from what an older generation placed on their shoulders. A dwarf’s departure can be as considered and determined as another dwarf’s decision to remain.

lore.label: If you want...
lore.text: If you want a character who can hold their ground, carry a difficult responsibility, and decide which commitments deserve that strength, play a dwarf.

lore.label: You Might...
lore.text:
• Inspect the support before trusting the impressive surface.
• Keep an old tool or ordinary object because of who used it before you.
• Show affection by doing the work someone else has been avoiding.

lore.label: Others Probably...
lore.text:
• Trust you to stay when a task turns unpleasant.
• Assume your certainty comes from experience rather than temperament.
• Wonder how long you intend to remember one careless remark.

lore.label: Physical Description (at a glance)
lore.text: Dwarves generally stand four to five feet tall, with broad torsos, sturdy joints, and a low center of balance. They are Medium despite their height. Hair, skin, and eye colors vary by lineage; thick hair and strong facial growth are common but differ between individuals and families. A dwarf’s clothing, beard styling, jewelry, and visible marks of belonging reflect their Culture and choices rather than an ancestry-wide uniform.

lore.label: Physical Description (lifecycle)
lore.text: Dwarves reach physical adulthood around twenty years and often live two to three centuries. They tend to retain strength well into later life, though age still brings injury, fatigue, and loss. Different cultures place different weight on years, experience, or the acceptance of a public responsibility when recognizing adulthood.

lore.label: Society
lore.text:
Dwarves inhabit mountain holds, river towns, cities, farms, and settlements alongside other peoples. Their work is as varied as the places they inhabit. In some communities with many dwarven families, a household is understood as a work carried across generations: its members might maintain a bridge, keep a garden, preserve a library, or support a trade. The obligation matters more than the material it involves.

Such arrangements can make reliable institutions and burdensome expectations. A family may expect a young dwarf to continue a work they never chose, or refuse to admit that a respected practice no longer serves anyone. Other communities deliberately pass important duties beyond blood relations, considering the person who keeps a thing working more significant than the name of its first maker.

lore.label: Beliefs
lore.text: Dwarven traditions often give spiritual weight to maintenance, honest workmanship, and obligations that can survive a bad year. A repaired roof may be a more convincing offering than an expensive ceremony. That outlook can serve many faiths, including those that have no connection to stone or metal. A dwarf may honor an ancestor by continuing their work, improving it, or finally correcting the harm it caused.

lore.label: Popular Edicts
lore.text:
• Make the thing sound before calling it finished.
• Carry the share you have agreed to carry.
• Teach someone how to maintain what you leave behind.

lore.label: Popular Anathemas
lore.text:
• Conceal a fault that will endanger another person.
• Claim the credit for work another hand completed.
• Demand endurance from others to spare yourself an honest change.

lore.label: Names
lore.text:
Many dwarven family names combine a material or descriptive word with part of a lasting structure: a span, vault, arch, pier, or lintel. The name may commemorate an ancestral home or public work rather than a current occupation. Given names are often short, with firm consonants.
• Common given names Bera, Dagna, Dorik, Helda, Korrin, Marda, Rurik, Torren.
• Common family names Broadarch, Deepvault, Highlintel, Ironspan, Redkeystone, Stonepier.

Elves are long-lived and keen-sensed, finding beauty in careful attention and difficulty in knowing when a thing is truly finished.

lore.label: Summary
lore.text: Elves are long-lived and keen-sensed, finding beauty in careful attention and difficulty in knowing when a thing is truly finished.

lore.label: About
lore.text:
An elf may remember the sapling beneath a spreading oak, the face on a weathered statue, and the first small quarrel behind a feud that now has its own songs. That memory changes how the world feels. A road is also the wood it replaced. A stranger’s expression may recall someone who died a century ago. Few things arrive without an echo.

Yet elves are as capable of impatience as anyone. Some spend years refining a small work because its imperfections will not leave them alone; others flee an old home because every doorway holds a conversation they can still hear. Their long lives offer time to change, but also time to become very certain that change is a mistake. An elf who takes to the road may be seeking something new, or finally accepting that something old is over.

lore.label: If you want...
lore.text: If you want a character whose long memory and careful senses make even familiar places feel layered with possibility, play an elf.

lore.label: You Might...
lore.text:
• Notice how a place has changed before asking who now owns it.
• Return to an unfinished craft, friendship, or promise after years away.
• Become fiercely attached to a short-lived companion’s plans.

lore.label: Others Probably...
lore.text:
• Mistake your deliberate attention for distraction or indifference.
• Ask you to remember a history you never personally witnessed.
• Wonder whether you are listening to them or to someone they remind you of.

lore.label: Physical Description (at a glance)
lore.text: Elves usually stand five and a half to six and a half feet tall, with long limbs, fine ears, and a light frame. Their coloring varies widely between families; eyes often show distinct rings or flecks that become clearer in dim light. Their movements tend to make small adjustments early, keeping a loose surface or crowded passage from becoming an obvious obstacle. Clothing and ornament follow upbringing, occupation, and personal taste.

lore.label: Physical Description (lifecycle)
lore.text: Elves reach physical adulthood at roughly twenty years. Many live three to five centuries, with rare elders surviving longer. Customs about adulthood vary by Culture, often marking the acceptance of responsibility or a first independent undertaking. Their memories remain fallible, and an old elf knows only the parts of history they actually lived or studied.

lore.label: Society
lore.text:
Elves live in cities, farm valleys, forest settlements, and communities shared with other ancestries. Their cultures govern their laws and loyalties. Where long-lived elven families gather, continuity often rests with people as much as with records: the same neighbor may witness several generations of a household’s agreements. This can preserve trust, but it can also preserve a grievance long after anyone else remembers its beginning.

Some elven households keep a place for returning members, expecting departures that would count as a lifetime elsewhere. Others deliberately move, rename themselves, or pass responsibility onward so the young are not forever waiting behind an elder. Among mixed communities, elves often learn the difficult habit of making decisions on someone else’s shorter timetable.

lore.label: Beliefs
lore.text: Elven beliefs are as varied as their cultures. Traditions with long elven histories often ask what deserves to continue and what should be allowed to end. A carefully maintained grove, a restored public square, and a song finally permitted to change may all express the same reverence. Some elves find comfort in cycles; others devote themselves to a particular life or work precisely because it will not return.

lore.label: Popular Edicts
lore.text:
• Give a person or a work your full attention.
• Preserve what others cannot afford to lose.
• Leave room for those who will follow you.

lore.label: Popular Anathemas
lore.text:
• Treat a short life as a lesser one.
• Keep a promise only because you have forgotten why it mattered.
• Destroy an irreplaceable thing through simple impatience.

lore.label: Names
lore.text:
Many elven naming traditions pair a flowing given name with a family name recalling a seasonal or celestial change. In Common, these family names often become two-part compounds such as Firstfrost or Rainwake. The name may recall an ancestor’s arrival, a remembered omen, or the season when a household began.
• Common given names Aelira, Calen, Elaris, Lethan, Meriel, Naeris, Orilan, Saelith.
• Common family names Dawnbloom, Firstfrost, Leafturn, Nightfall, Rainwake, Sunwane.

Gnomes are perceptive and resilient, with a lasting sensitivity to the unusual and a capacity for attention that can make a small detail occupy an entire afternoon.

lore.label: Summary
lore.text: Gnomes are perceptive and resilient, with a lasting sensitivity to the unusual and a capacity for attention that can make a small detail occupy an entire afternoon.

lore.label: About
lore.text:
A gnome may notice a slight change in a voice, a hairline seam in a well-made object, or a pattern that only appears when everyone else has stopped looking. Some turn that attention toward machines or magic; others toward gardens, people, music, law, or a question so narrow that its importance takes time to explain. An interest can outlast a working life and follow its owner through several changes of vocation.

Old stories connect gnomes with places where the world behaves a little differently: lights without a flame, paths that seem shorter on the return journey, voices heard through the wrong wall. Their inherited resistance to mental influence lends those stories weight, though it does not prove any one account. Gnomes can be practical about the uncanny and hopelessly speculative about an ordinary loose hinge. They become adventurers for the same varied reasons anyone does, with the added possibility that the unanswered question has finally moved somewhere dangerous.

lore.label: If you want...
lore.text: If you want a character who notices the odd detail, follows an interest seriously, and can bring an unusual perspective to a familiar problem, play a gnome.

lore.label: You Might...
lore.text:
• Ask a precise question that changes what everyone thought they understood.
• Keep a small object because its construction or history still puzzles you.
• Become deeply competent in a subject that first caught your attention by accident.

lore.label: Others Probably...
lore.text:
• Confuse your intense interest with an inability to take anything seriously.
• Bring you a mystery when they meant to ask for a simple repair.
• Discover that you remember the small thing they said months ago.

lore.label: Physical Description (at a glance)
lore.text: Gnomes generally stand two and a half to three and a half feet tall. They are Small, with expressive faces, fine ears, and alert eyes. Skin, hair, and eye colors vary widely; some lineages show unusual saturated tones or a faint luminous sheen. These features need not be bright or conspicuous. Dress, ornament, and the tools a gnome carries reflect their Culture and work rather than an ancestry-wide taste for tinkering.

lore.label: Physical Description (lifecycle)
lore.text: Gnomes reach physical adulthood around twenty years and commonly live one hundred eighty to two hundred fifty years. Their interests may change many times over that span, or deepen around a single enduring pursuit. Age brings physical changes and personal losses. Some elders seek fresh pursuits; others find a settled pleasure in familiar work and the people who have come to share it.

lore.label: Society
lore.text:
Gnomes live in mixed cities, quiet rural settlements, river communities, and places of their own making. Their laws and institutions come from their cultures. In communities with many gnomish households, informal networks often gather around shared interests: a survey, a musical tradition, an old court case, or the careful observation of one hillside. Such groups can outlast the problem that brought them together.

Attention can be generous or possessive. One gnome may welcome anyone who can add a useful observation, while another guards a modest discovery as though it were a royal inheritance. Long-running projects sometimes become the easiest route into a community and the hardest thing to leave. Adventuring gnomes often carry a promise to bring back a specimen, an answer, or simply an account that someone at home will understand.

lore.label: Beliefs
lore.text: Gnomish traditions often value careful observation, honest wonder, and the obligation to admit when a cherished explanation fails. Some faiths understand discovery as a form of devotion; others emphasize tending the mysteries that should not be disturbed. A gnome’s sensitivity to the uncanny can lead to reverence, skepticism, or a very practical desire to know which door should remain closed.

lore.label: Popular Edicts
lore.text:
• Look closely before deciding that a thing is ordinary.
• Share a discovery with someone who can make good use of it.
• Change your explanation when the evidence demands it.

lore.label: Popular Anathemas
lore.text:
• Make a person the unwilling subject of your curiosity.
• Hide a dangerous flaw to protect the elegance of an idea.
• Dismiss another person’s interest merely because it is small or unfamiliar.

lore.label: Names
lore.text:
Some gnomish families favor alliterative names. Their translated family names often pair a material with a small object or component, preserving the memory of an old discovery, project, or household curiosity. A pleasing sound can follow a family for generations after the original object or project has been forgotten.
• Common given names Bimri, Della, Fenna, Nori, Perri, Sella, Tessa, Venn.
• Common family names Brasshinge, Dewglass, Flintwheel, Needlespring, Pewterpin, Tinspire.

Halflings are small and adaptable, often finding that an attentive hand and a fortunate second chance can turn the course of a much larger problem.

lore.label: Summary
lore.text: Halflings are small and adaptable, often finding that an attentive hand and a fortunate second chance can turn the course of a much larger problem.

lore.label: About
lore.text:
Halflings live close to a world built by larger people. A countertop can hide a conversation; a hurried crowd can become moving walls; a door made for someone else may require both hands. Familiarity with such inconveniences often produces a practical eye for another approach. A halfling notices the smaller latch, the loose board, or the person nobody thought to ask.

Their reputed luck is harder to explain. A slipping grip catches again. A lock yields at the last adjustment. The bridge plank breaks one step behind them. Halflings disagree about whether this is a blessing, an inherited gift, or a story people tell after forgetting all the careful work that preceded it. None of those explanations guarantees an easy life, and many halflings become adventurers because they are tired of being someone else’s reassuring little exception.

lore.label: If you want...
lore.text: If you want a character whose small stature leaves plenty of room for resourcefulness, courage, and the occasional unlikely escape, play a halfling.

lore.label: You Might...
lore.text:
• Notice who has been overlooked in a crowded room.
• Keep a modest comfort ready for an uncertain journey.
• Try a practical approach after an imposing one has failed.

lore.label: Others Probably...
lore.text:
• Underestimate how far you have already traveled.
• Tell the story of your escape as though luck did all the work.
• Relax around you before realizing how closely you have been paying attention.

lore.label: Physical Description (at a glance)
lore.text: Halflings usually stand two and a half to three and a half feet tall. They are Small, with varied builds, rounded or lightly pointed ears, and hands capable of very precise work. Broad feet and dense hair on the lower legs occur in many families; well-fitted boots and sturdy sandals are as common as bare feet. Their clothing and household arrangements follow the Culture and surroundings in which they live.

lore.label: Physical Description (lifecycle)
lore.text: Halflings reach physical adulthood at around eighteen years. Many live between one hundred and one hundred sixty years, with some surviving longer. Their physical development resembles that of humans more closely than that of the very long-lived peoples, while their extended later years let them remain part of several generations of a household.

lore.label: Society
lore.text:
Halflings build their own settlements and live throughout the towns and countries of other peoples. Their families may be established farmers, urban tenants, river travelers, court officials, or anything else their Culture and circumstances allow. Communities with many halfling households often pay close attention to shared access: a low latch, an extra step, and a place to sit are signs that someone has considered who will actually use a room.

Some households preserve belonging through regular meals and visits; others through routes, letters, and the expectation that a traveler can return without explaining every year away. This welcome can become intrusive when a family decides it knows what kind of life should make a person content. A halfling who leaves may be carrying the household’s hopes, escaping them, or simply curious about what lies beyond the familiar turn in the road.

lore.label: Beliefs
lore.text: Many halfling traditions give significance to ordinary acts of welcome, safe passage, and remembering the absent. Luck may be addressed as a spirit, a blessing, an ancestor’s attention, or a habit of staying alert. Their beliefs can be solemn, skeptical, or exuberant. The familiar emphasis on small comforts is often an acknowledgment that security requires work, not proof that the world is harmless.

lore.label: Popular Edicts
lore.text:
• Make room for someone the room was not built to welcome.
• Share what keeps you steady through a difficult day.
• Give a good effort the chance to become a fortunate one.

lore.label: Popular Anathemas
lore.text:
• Mistake another person’s small stature for a small claim to respect.
• Take hospitality and repay it with contempt.
• Rely on luck to excuse a danger you could have prevented.

lore.label: Names
lore.text:
Many halfling family names remember a small landmark near an ancestral home: a gate, lane, stile, ford, or turn in a road. In Common they often combine a plant or local feature with that landmark. The family need not still live there.
• Common given names Bessa, Jory, Milo, Nell, Orrin, Pella, Tamsin, Tobin.
• Common family names Barleybridge, Brackenstile, Hazelturn, Littleford, Reedgate, Sunlane.

Serrovanians build trust through witnessed promises, careful records, and the conviction that a person should answer for their word.

lore.label: Summary
lore.text: Serrovanians build trust through witnessed promises, careful records, and the conviction that a person should answer for their word.

lore.label: About
lore.text:
Serrovane is a lowland order-state of cultivated fields, raised roads, and towns gathered around registry halls. Its ledgers are kept in triplicate, its agreements carry witnesses, and its disputes follow forms that everyone is expected to respect. A promise spoken casually may be forgotten. A promise entered into the record becomes something other people can build their lives upon.

People of many ancestries belong to this order. An elven witness, a dwarven magistrate, and a human challenger may disagree bitterly while trusting the same record. Serrovanians learn how to state a grievance, acknowledge an obligation, and offer a concession without surrendering their standing. They can be formidable negotiators: they know exactly what they have promised, and they expect you to know the same.

lore.label: If you want...
lore.text: If you want a character who takes promises seriously, understands the power of public reputation, and can turn a few carefully chosen words into a lasting obligation, choose Serrovane.

lore.label: You Might...
lore.text:
• Ask who witnessed an agreement before asking whether it was a good one.
• Carry copies of important promises, judgments, or introductions among your belongings.
• Insist on settling the terms of a contest before anyone draws a weapon.

lore.label: Others Probably...
lore.text:
• Trust you to remember an obligation long after everyone else has forgotten it.
• Find your careful questions reassuring, exhausting, or faintly threatening.
• Worry that an innocent remark might become a commitment in your hearing.

lore.label: Dress and Bearing
lore.text:
Serrovanian clothing favors orderly layers, durable fabrics, and visible signs of affiliation. Household colors, office badges, and witness cords help others recognize whom a person represents. Garments vary with ancestry, occupation, and means, but people generally take care that closures are secure and identifying marks remain legible.

Formal bearing matters as much as fine clothing. Standing to acknowledge a witness, leaving another speaker room to finish, and presenting a document with clean hands all communicate respect.

lore.label: Upbringing and Milestones
lore.text:
Children learn promises through ordinary responsibilities: returning borrowed tools, delivering messages accurately, and admitting when a task remains unfinished. Many households preserve a young person’s first independently witnessed obligation.

Public responsibility follows demonstrated judgment, with its timing shaped by ancestry and family custom. Taking an office, joining a household, completing an apprenticeship, and retiring from service are commonly marked by a formal acknowledgment of the duties being accepted or released.

lore.label: Society
lore.text:
Serrovanian institutions depend on recorded responsibilities. Officials swear to the limits of their offices, guilds preserve the terms of their charters, and households keep accounts of debts, inheritances, and obligations. Public scribes and witnesses are familiar figures in markets and village squares.

Formal challenge gives disputes an accepted shape. The grievance, the contest, and the consequences are declared before witnesses. Some challenges involve arms; others test skill, testimony, or the ability to substantiate a claim. Violence within accepted terms can be lawful. Breaking those terms threatens the trust that made the challenge possible.

This order has its cruelties. Wealth buys patient advocates, old records can preserve old injustices, and a precisely worded agreement can conceal an ugly intention. Serrovanians argue fiercely over whether justice lies in honoring the record or correcting what should never have been written into it.

lore.label: Beliefs
lore.text:
Serrovanians follow many faiths, but promises, testimony, and remembrance occupy an honored place across them. Shrines often witness marriages, reconciliations, and vows of service. An ancestor may be remembered through an obligation their descendants continue to uphold.

Mercy also has a recognized dignity. Publicly releasing someone from an oath can be an act of generosity remembered as long as the oath itself.

lore.label: Popular Edicts
lore.text:
• Keep your word when doing so becomes inconvenient.
• State your terms before the contest begins.
• Stand witness when another needs the truth recorded.

lore.label: Popular Anathemas
lore.text:
• Knowingly swear an oath you intend to break.
• Falsify a record entrusted to your care.
• Inflict punishment beyond the terms of an accepted challenge.

lore.label: Names
lore.text:
Many Serrovanian surnames take the form of a short promise: something a household declares it will uphold. These names are inherited, and families take particular pride in living up to them. Someone named Speaktrue can expect a lie to be remembered with unusual clarity.

People commonly retain given names from their family or ancestry. The surnames below are familiar Common translations of Serrovine names.
• Common given names Cerran, Dovra, Ilyra, Maroven, Orven, Selka, Tavren, Veyra.

system.description: Reachers thrive where people and possibilities meet, building livelihoods through sharp observation, useful introductions, and bargains worth making again.

lore.label: Summary
lore.text: Reachers thrive where people and possibilities meet, building livelihoods through sharp observation, useful introductions, and bargains worth making again.

lore.label: About
lore.text:
Kestrel Reach spreads across a wide river delta, where channels divide around crowded islands and trade-towns rise above the floodwater. Six languages may be spoken along a single dock, with three more heard by evening. Boats bring unfamiliar goods, travelers bring unfamiliar customs, and someone is always looking for a person who understands both.

Reachers grow accustomed to difference early. An elven shipwright, a dwarven grain factor, and a human ferryman may share a neighborhood, a business venture, and a running argument about harbor fees. Local knowledge means knowing how people prefer to be approached, which courtesies matter to them, and whom they trust to make an introduction. A good broker can accomplish with an afternoon’s conversation what an armed company might spend a season making worse.

lore.label: If you want...
lore.text: If you want a character who is comfortable among unfamiliar faces, always listening for an opportunity, and rarely without someone they could ask for help, choose Kestrel Reach.

lore.label: You Might...
lore.text:
• Learn a few useful words whenever you encounter a new language.
• Introduce yourself by naming someone the other person already knows.
• Look for what each side needs before deciding that a dispute cannot be settled.

lore.label: Others Probably...
lore.text:
• Expect you to know a useful contact in almost any port.
• Wonder whether your friendly questions are leading toward a proposal.
• Rely on you to notice the custom, omission, or hidden cost they overlooked.

lore.label: Dress and Bearing
lore.text:
Reach clothing reflects crowded docks, changeable weather, and goods arriving from distant places. Practical layers, secure pockets, broad hats, and garments kept clear of ropes are common. Fabrics and ornaments travel freely between communities, adapted to each wearer’s build and family traditions.

Reachers often display a token of their trade, vessel, or trading house where an acquaintance can recognize it. Greeting gestures vary between neighborhoods, and knowing which one to offer can make a warmer introduction than expensive clothes.

lore.label: Upbringing and Milestones
lore.text:
Young Reachers learn by carrying messages, helping with household business, and accompanying experienced relatives through markets and landing places. They are taught to notice who has spoken, who has been overlooked, and whether everyone understands the same terms.

A first independently completed bargain or entrusted journey often marks growing responsibility. Its importance lies in returning with the agreement fulfilled and the other party willing to deal with the household again. These milestones follow readiness and circumstance across the Reach’s many ancestries.

lore.label: Society
lore.text:
The delta depends on cooperation that extends beyond individual towns. Ferrymen need maintained channels, merchants need dependable warehouses, and everyone needs the flood banks to hold. Neighborhood associations, trading houses, craft guilds, and harbor officials overlap in a web of favors and competing responsibilities.

Reputation moves quickly along the waterways. A generous settlement can bring business from three towns away; a cheated customer can arrive ahead of you wherever you hoped to trade next. Brokers earn their standing by remembering details, protecting confidences, and finding terms that people will actually honor.

The Reach’s friendliness can conceal hard boundaries. Established houses sometimes keep profitable routes among themselves, and an introduction may matter more than an excellent offer. Reachers admire people who open opportunities for others, but they also know how easily a well-connected few can decide who gets a place at the table.

lore.label: Beliefs
lore.text:
Reach shrines welcome travelers, returning crews, and families whose traditions came from elsewhere. River spirits, ancestral patrons, and gods of craft, fortune, and safe passage all receive offerings.

Many Reachers regard hospitality as an obligation that travels. Someone shelters a stranger today because another household may shelter their own kin tomorrow. Gifts, favors, and acts of kindness create relationships whose value cannot always be entered into an account.

lore.label: Popular Edicts
lore.text:
• Learn how to greet people on their own terms.
• Give the other party a reason to trade with you again.
• Share a useful introduction when it costs you little.

lore.label: Popular Anathemas
lore.text:
• Abuse the protection offered to a guest.
• Conceal a danger that makes an agreement impossible to fulfill.
• Betray a confidence entrusted to you as a broker.

lore.label: Names
lore.text:
Reach surnames often come from waterways and shoreline features. A name may remember the bank where a household built its first home, the channel its boats worked, or the landing from which its members scattered across the world. Families carry these names inland long after the river itself has become a distant memory.

Given names mingle freely across languages and ancestries. The surnames below are commonly used in their Common forms.
• Common given names Avi, Dena, Jori, Kes, Lio, Mira, Neris, Orren, Savi, Tavi.
• Common surnames Broadwater, Lowbank, Northbank, Reedbank, Siltwater, Stillwater, Three-Tides, Willowbend.
• Example names Avi Northbank, Dena Willowbend, Jori Reedbank, Mira Three-Tides, Neris Stillwater, Tavi Lowbank.

system.description: Cairnwarders share the work that keeps a mountain road passable, a shelter supplied, and a struggling traveler from being left behind.

lore.label: Summary
lore.text: Cairnwarders share the work that keeps a mountain road passable, a shelter supplied, and a struggling traveler from being left behind.

lore.label: About
lore.text:
Cairnward is a chain of high valleys and pass towns joined by narrow roads, rope bridges, and stone shelters whose doors open from the outside. Snow can close a route between breakfast and dusk. Every settlement therefore maintains places where a stranger can find dry fuel, a blanket, and directions to the next safe roof. The supplies belong to the road, and taking what you need creates an expectation that you will replenish a shelter when you can.

People of many ancestries keep this system working. A halfling may inspect a bridge’s underside while a dwarf anchors the line, an elf reads a changing sky, and a gnome counts the fuel left at the next refuge. Cairnwarders learn that useful strength includes knowing when to ask for another pair of hands. The region admires a difficult rescue, but admires the uneventful journey made possible by good maintenance just as much.

lore.label: If you want...
lore.text: If you want a character who judges a community by whom it is prepared to help, shares difficult work readily, and knows the value of a safe place to stop, choose Cairnward.

lore.label: You Might...
lore.text:
• Check how much fuel and food remain before settling into a borrowed shelter.
• Divide a difficult load before anyone has to admit that it is too heavy.
• Leave a clear warning where the next traveler will see it.

lore.label: Others Probably...
lore.text:
• Trust you to notice when someone is quietly falling behind.
• Find your questions about ropes, weather, and spare blankets excessive until the road turns bad.
• Assume you will help, and sometimes forget to ask what that help costs you.

lore.label: Dress and Bearing
lore.text:
Cairnward clothing favors repairable layers, close-fitting sleeves, and cords that can be handled with cold fingers. Bright shoulder tabs make travelers easier to count in fog or snow. Different towns favor different colors, while a small braided loop commonly identifies a household that helps maintain a particular route. Garments and equipment are fitted to their wearer’s ancestry and build.

Offering someone the sheltered side of a doorway is a familiar courtesy. So is taking one end of a load before beginning a long conversation. Elaborate clothing earns little admiration if its owner refuses to mend a loose fastening.

lore.label: Upbringing and Milestones
lore.text:
Children begin with small contributions: carrying a handful of kindling to a nearby refuge, learning the warning signs, and accompanying adults on a short maintenance walk. They are taught to distinguish a task they can manage from one that needs help.

A first independently completed shelter round often marks growing responsibility. The young person returns with an account of what was repaired, replaced, or left for a more experienced crew. Ancestry, ability, and circumstance shape the timing. Later milestones include taking responsibility for a route, teaching a new crew, and handing a demanding duty onward before age or injury makes it unsafe.

lore.label: Society
lore.text:
Cairnward’s towns govern their own affairs but share responsibility for the routes between them. Seasonal gatherings assign shelter rounds, bridge inspections, and repair crews. Contributions may be labor, materials, food, transport, or skilled planning. A person who cannot safely climb a pass can still arrange the work that makes it passable.

Rescue crews are assembled around the situation rather than inherited office. The most experienced person for the route leads, and others are expected to speak when they notice a danger. Once everyone is home, the community replaces damaged equipment and supports those injured in its service.

The system can also make unreasonable demands. A capable household may receive every difficult assignment while a wealthy one supplies goods and keeps its members safe at home. Families sometimes pressure an exhausted rescuer to prove their loyalty one more time. Cairnwarders argue over how to share danger fairly, and who must be heard when a respected leader says the risk is acceptable.

lore.label: Beliefs
lore.text:
Cairnward shelters often contain a small shared shrine, though the people who maintain them follow many faiths. Travelers leave a knot, a stone, or a few words of thanks after reaching safety. Those lost on the road are remembered by name, with particular care taken to mark where a rescue failed or a route changed.

Many Cairnwarders understand care for an unknown future traveler as a form of devotion. A dry blanket left behind can serve that purpose as readily as a prayer spoken aloud.

lore.label: Popular Edicts
lore.text:
• Leave the shelter ready for the person who comes after you.
• Share the load before it breaks someone.
• Mark a danger clearly, even when you cannot repair it yourself.

lore.label: Popular Anathemas
lore.text:
• Take a refuge’s last supplies and conceal the shortage.
• Move or falsify a trusted waymark for personal advantage.
• Pressure someone into a rescue whose danger you refuse to share.

lore.label: Names
lore.text:
Cairnward household names often pair a number with a useful provision. Such a name remembers the painted sign of an old refuge, the gift that established a household, or the supplies its members once promised to maintain. The number is a remembered emblem rather than a current inventory. Adopted relatives and people who join a household commonly take its name.

Given names often come from family and ancestry traditions. Common forms of the household names are used below.
• Common given names Anya, Bera, Elda, Fenna, Kellan, Meriel, Pella, Torek.
• Common household names Five-Blankets, Four-Cups, Nine-Ropes, Seven-Coals, Three-Loaves, Two-Lanterns.

system.description: Lethrans learn to read the part a person is playing, signal across a crowded room, and move gracefully between public duties and private lives.

lore.label: Summary
lore.text: Lethrans learn to read the part a person is playing, signal across a crowded room, and move gracefully between public duties and private lives.

lore.label: About
lore.text:
Lethra is a terraced hill city and its surrounding towns, known for shaded lanes, lantern courts, and the public masks hung beside the doors of neighborhood halls. A service mask identifies a duty. The Open Palm hears a dispute, the Lantern Eye guides people through the night, and the White Reed carries an entrusted message. Qualified residents take turns wearing them, so a familiar office may have a different voice or stature tomorrow.

The custom gives people a way to serve without making every public act a test of family standing. An elven mediator, a dwarven messenger, and a halfling night guide may wear masks recognized across the same quarter. Private faces are greeted by name; public masks are addressed by their duties. Festivals turn that habit into theater, with neighbors borrowing parts, exchanging costumes, and enjoying how much a small change of bearing can alter a familiar person.

lore.label: If you want...
lore.text: If you want a character who understands the power of a convincing role, protects room for a private self, and can turn a crowded scene into an opportunity for a companion, choose Lethra.

lore.label: You Might...
lore.text:
• Ask what duty a person is performing before deciding how to address them.
• Use a small gesture to cue a companion across a noisy room.
• Keep a change of clothing or a carefully maintained mask among your belongings.

lore.label: Others Probably...
lore.text:
• Expect you to notice a false note in someone’s manner.
• Wonder which parts of your public confidence you carry into private life.
• Rely on you to draw attention when someone else needs a moment to act.

lore.label: Dress and Bearing
lore.text:
Lethran clothing favors garments that can be adjusted, layered, and moved in easily. Reversible coats, detachable collars, and bright linings let a person change their public presentation without replacing an entire wardrobe. Masks are fitted to the wearer: beards, ears, spectacles, and different facial shapes all receive practical consideration.

Service masks use established designs; festival masks invite invention. Lethrans generally leave another person’s mask alone unless invited to handle it. Removing one’s own mask at the end of a duty is a small but deliberate acknowledgment that the office has been put aside.

lore.label: Upbringing and Milestones
lore.text:
Children learn public roles through games, errands, and supervised festival performances. A game may require them to deliver an accurate message while pretending to be someone else, or to recognize a familiar adult from posture alone. They also learn when a shared joke has made another person uncomfortable.

A first public duty is usually undertaken with an experienced partner. Acceptance depends on readiness, training, and the demands of the role across Lethra’s many ancestries. Taking a service mask, returning it after a final term, and teaching its next wearer are widely recognized milestones.

lore.label: Society
lore.text:
Neighborhood maskhouses maintain the service masks, train their wearers, and arrange rotating duties. Residents can bring a complaint against an office without knowing the wearer’s private name. The maskhouse is responsible for examining the complaint and putting right harm done in its service; the wearer remains answerable for deliberate abuse.

Public performance supports ordinary civic life. Announcements, petitions, and difficult disagreements are often presented in open courts where people are accustomed to attending closely and responding in turn. A well-timed pause or an offered change of speaker can keep an argument from becoming a contest of volume.

The system has its failures. Established maskhouses may decide who is qualified before an outsider ever receives a fair hearing, and an admired office can shelter a disappointing wearer. A convincing false mask can exploit public trust. Lethrans debate how much privacy an officeholder should retain, and how to expose wrongdoing without turning every public duty into a spectacle.

lore.label: Beliefs
lore.text:
Lethra’s faiths approach masks in different ways. Some use them to represent divine duties, ancestral figures, or the changing seasons. Others insist that worship begins when every mask is set aside. Both kinds of shrine can stand in the same street.

A common act of remembrance is to repair an object used in someone’s public service and offer it to a new wearer. The dead person is named during the gift, preserving their contribution while leaving the next person room to serve in their own way.

lore.label: Popular Edicts
lore.text:
• Perform the duty you have agreed to represent.
• Give another person room to put a public role aside.
• Use attention carefully, especially when a quieter voice needs to be heard.

lore.label: Popular Anathemas
lore.text:
• Claim the authority of a service mask you have no right to wear.
• Expose a private confidence merely to entertain an audience.
• Let a respected office excuse deliberate harm by its wearer.

lore.label: Names
lore.text:
Many Lethran family names combine a color with part of a garment. The name may recall the costume of an old household festival role, a family’s traditional colors, or an ancestor’s recognizable public dress. These inherited names remain in use after the original garment has been lost. They confer no office or authority.

Given names often retain the sounds of a family’s ancestry or home language. The surnames below use their familiar Common translations.
• Common given names Della, Elaris, Jori, Lio, Marda, Neri, Sella, Tavin.
• Common surnames Bluesleeve, Goldcuff, Grayhem, Greencollar, Redsash, Whiteribbon.

You become Trained in Athletics and Intimidation, and you become Trained in a relevant Lore of your choice.

Example Lores include Arena Fighting Lore, Prizefights Lore, Lore of a fighting circuit.
system.description: You fought for purses, wagers, or someone else’s profit. You learned how to frighten an opponent before the first exchange and how to keep standing when the crowd demanded more.

system.specialAbility:
You become Trained in Crafting and Performance, and you become Trained in a relevant Lore of your choice.

Example Lores include Puppetry Lore, Stage Mechanisms Lore, Theater Lore.
system.description: You built figures and gave them a life before an audience. You learned how a small movement could hold a room's attention and how to repair a tangled mechanism before anyone noticed.

system.specialAbility:
You become Trained in Athletics and Survival, and you become Trained in a relevant Lore of your choice.

Example Lores include Sailing Lore, River Navigation Lore, Lore of a particular coastline.
system.description: You worked aboard a vessel where an unsecured line could cost a life. Weather and hard voyages taught you to keep your footing and trust the people working beside you.

system.specialAbility:
You become Trained in Insight and Society, and you become Trained in a relevant Lore of your choice.

Example Lores include Lore of a region's history, Astronomy Lore, Lore of an ancient civilization.
system.description: You studied old accounts and disputed their meaning with people just as certain as you were. An unanswered question eventually gave you a reason to leave the safety of your books.

system.specialAbility:
You become Trained in Crafting and Insight, and you become Trained in a relevant Lore of your choice.

Example Lores include Calligraphy Lore, Bookbinding Lore, Lore of a particular archive.
system.description: You copied and preserved documents, learning to recognize a careless source and mend a damaged page. Somewhere among other people's words, you found a matter that demanded action.

system.specialAbility:
You become Trained in Insight and Stealth, and you become Trained in a relevant Lore of your choice.

Example Lores include Household Management Lore, Etiquette Lore, Lore of a prominent household.
system.description: You worked in a household where remaining useful often meant remaining unnoticed. You learned its routines, soothed its tempers, and discovered how much people reveal when they forget who is in the room.

system.specialAbility:
You become Trained in Athletics and Intimidation, and you become Trained in a relevant Lore of your choice.

Example Lores include Military Logistics Lore, Siegecraft Lore, Fortifications Lore, Lore of a particular army or campaign.
system.description: You served in somebody's army: a levy, a free company, a city watch that saw real fighting. You learned the drill, the marching, and the waiting, and you learned what a line looks like just before it breaks.

system.specialAbility:
You become Trained in Animal Handling and Athletics, and you become Trained in a relevant Lore of your choice.

Example Lores include Stabling Lore, Animal Husbandry Lore, Equine Anatomy Lore.
system.description: You cared for mounts and worked wherever a stable needed strong hands. You learned to approach a nervous animal patiently and recognize trouble before a saddle ever touched its back.

system.specialAbility:
You become Trained in Stealth and Survival, and you become Trained in a relevant Lore of your choice.

Example Lores include Hunting Lore, Trapping Lore, Lore of a wilderness region.
system.description: You made your living following tracks and setting snares far from settled roads. Patience put food on your table, and quiet movement kept you from becoming something else’s meal.

system.specialAbility:
You become Trained in Insight and Intimidation, and you become Trained in a relevant Lore of your choice.

Example Lores include City Watch Lore, Patrol Routes Lore, Local Law Lore.
system.description: You kept watch where a quiet street could turn dangerous without warning. You learned to read a gathering crowd and make your authority felt before a quarrel became a fight.

system.specialAbility: Sneak Attack: +1d6 precision damage vs. Off-Guard foes, rising to +2d6 at Expert, +3d6 at Master, and +4d6 at Legendary.
system.description: Grants Training in Stealth, and 8 Opening Vigor, added once if it is your first Calling.

system.specialAbility: Rage ❶: Temporary Vigor equal to your level + Might, +2 melee damage, −1 Evade, and you are Heedless while it lasts. The damage rises to +4 at Expert, +6 at Master, +8 at Legendary.
system.description: Grants Training in Athletics, and 12 Opening Vigor, added once if it is your first Calling.

system.specialAbility: Panache: held on a critical Strike, a Feint, or a Demoralize; +1 Situation to Evade and +1 ft to your Speeds while you hold it (Speed +2 ft at Expert, Evade +2 at Master, Speed +3 ft at Legendary).
system.description: Grants Training in Acrobatics, and 10 Opening Vigor, added once if it is your first Calling.

system.specialAbility: Mark Prey ❶: +1d8 precision damage the first time each round you Hit your prey (2d8 at Expert, 3d8 at Master, 4d8 at Legendary), and you always know roughly where it is within 60 feet.
system.description: Grants Training in Awareness, and 10 Opening Vigor, added once if it is your first Calling.

system.specialAbility: Drilled: Weapon Familiarity free; treat your Melee or Ranged Proficiency Bonus as 2 higher with that Weapon Group; and you may take Reactive Strike without being Expert in Melee.
system.description: Grants Training in Athletics, and 10 Opening Vigor, added once if it is your first Calling.

system.specialAbility: Spellshaping: once per round, add ❶ to a Cast you know to extend its range by 5 feet, or to move one square of its area; your first Calling also trains you in a magical discipline.
system.description: Grants Training in Guile, and 6 Opening Vigor, added once if it is your first Calling.

system.specialAbility: Blood Price: once per round, lose 1 + the discipline's Damage Dice in Vigor as you declare a damaging Cast; if it Hits, one creature takes that much more.
system.description: Grants Training in Athletics, and 8 Opening Vigor, added once if it is your first Calling.

system.specialAbility: Death Echo: once per round, when a living creature within 15 feet takes a Wound or becomes Spent, hold an Echo; spend it before a Strike or damaging Cast for +2 damage on a Hit.
system.description: Grants Training in Awareness, and 8 Opening Vigor, added once if it is your first Calling.

system.specialAbility: Call Manifestation ❷: one 1-foot manifestation within 6 feet, lasting the encounter; Command ❶ it to Move or make a 1d4 Zoned Strike. It vanishes on a Hit.
system.description: Grants Training in Awareness, and 6 Opening Vigor, added once if it is your first Calling.

system.specialAbility: Spellbound Edge ❶: your next Deliberate Melee Strike deals a known spell's damage type instead of its own. Needs Melee and a magical discipline.
system.description: Grants Training in Athletics, and 8 Opening Vigor, added once if it is your first Calling.
